factory-reform--tomioka.text: Both cases show that industrial change needed skilled people. Teaching reeling at Tomioka can document how a technique spread. An inspector’s report can document how a British complaint was investigated. They answer different questions about working conditions.
sections: An inspector had to investigate what happened
A machine still needs practiced hands

banda-1621--manila-network.text: Shipbuilding and repairs in the Manila system and cultivating and processing spices on Banda reveal the work behind trade. A colonial report on an imposed monopoly cannot speak for the Bandanese, and wreck cargo cannot measure consent among Philippine workers.
sections: Plantation production depended on people’s knowledge
Royal construction placed burdens on communities

isfahan-silk--bukhara-books.text: A merchant family’s letter makes separation visible at New Julfa, while manuscript and endowment records identify bookmaking and maintenance in Bukhara. Each reflects people with access to particular institutions. Neither represents every urban household.
sections: Commerce required relationships and information
Water and income sustained institutions

isfahan-silk--zand-iran.text: The carpet’s possible production centres and the lacquer case’s attributed painter offer different degrees of identification. Accounts of Safavid Isfahan and later Zand Shiraz provide context without revealing either object’s particular purchaser or workshop.
sections: Silk connected several kinds of making
One object, several kinds of evidence

ming-workshops--ottoman-workshops.text: The Ming vessel’s reign mark and an Ottoman decorator’s name identify different relationships to production. Court designs, commissions, workshop debris and market records provide separate checks on whether an item was ordered, made or bought.
sections: An official order needed more than a design
Names and production remains

mughal-books--ottoman-workshops.text: A Mughal manuscript project organized translators, writers and painters. An Ottoman object can preserve a decorator’s name, while production debris records other tasks. Individuals named in either setting provide only part of a workshop’s history.
sections: Different skills made a book possible
Names and production remains

chaco-communities--ocmulgee-council.text: Masonry and food remains at Chaco and modeled clay at Ocmulgee show people building and using places. Dates belong to particular structures or samples. A later council account adds living significance without identifying every ancient institution.
sections: Materials made different spaces possible
Retained material makes new questions possible

cahokia-city--ocmulgee-council.text: Cahokia’s changing neighborhoods and unfinished copper show work at particular locations. At Ocmulgee a revised building chronology and community accounts add other kinds of evidence. Neither settlement stands for the history of every descendant community.
sections: Homes within an urban landscape
Living relationships shape research

byzantium--borobudur.text: Harbour timbers record practical repair at Constantinople, while Borobudur’s galleries and drainage reveal construction and later maintenance. The devotional ivory and modern conservation add context at different dates. Neither establishes the full workforce behind a monument.
sections: Fitting and maintaining a working hull
Moving water required continued work

byzantium--maya-vessel.text: Both portable objects invite questions about purpose and access. A Maya cup can name its owner. The ivory’s devotional use depends on interpretation. Separate household and harbour excavations cannot identify the workshop for either object.
sections: Carving a portable image
Naming a relationship

dongson--hopewell-earthworks.text: In Vietnam a group of tools inside a drum documents one deposit. In Ohio a trench and an early plan document particular earthwork features. Later moulds or a modern community account add dated perspectives without establishing one purpose or linked route.
sections: Objects were gathered into particular groups
A wall preserves a particular sequence

colima--hopewell-earthworks.text: A Colima model preserves roof and stair forms. A separately excavated tomb supplies an association; Ohio earthwork plans and trenches record built features. A reconstruction at either scale needs evidence beyond resemblance and cannot supply the model’s exact findspot.
sections: Preparing places and gifts
Building, dismantling and adding earth

chavin-textile--teotihuacan.text: The cloth preserves threads and pigment but has only a reported regional origin. Tlajinga’s excavated compounds place blade-making debris in a particular neighborhood. This supports a comparison of work while leaving the cloth maker’s location unknown.
sections: A surface was made before an image was painted
A household could also make tools

chavin-textile--moche.text: Painted woven cloth and modeled or painted pottery both register deliberate material choices. Debris at Huacas de Moche places some pottery work in a workshop, while the textile’s reported origin leaves its production site open.
sections: A surface was made before an image was painted
Making more than decorated bottles

indonesia-independence--ghana-independen.text: Both cases separate a declaration or constitutional change from the distribution of political power. Indonesia’s proclamation, federal settlement and unitary state took different steps from Ghana’s independence under a monarchy and subsequent republic. Neither sequence measures every citizen’s freedom.
sections: Negotiating the shape of the state
Independence did not mean one opinion

ghana-independence--south-africa-rights.text: Ghana’s independence and later republic changed the state’s form. In South Africa the election, signing and commencement of the constitution mark distinct steps. A transfer of power or the existence of a constitutional right still leaves its exercise to be investigated.
sections: Follow the promise into the institutions
Adoption, review, signing and commencement

roman-world--eastern-han.text: Both empires depended on provision beyond the court. Han tomb granaries represent an estate’s imagined supplies. A Roman imperial portrait presents legitimacy. Neither shows how much ordinary producers supplied, and the earlier Han debates predate the Eastern Han models.
sections: The work that supported imperial life
An estate is a network of work

eastern-han--colima.text: Both miniature buildings select features of larger structures. Han funerary models represent provision for the afterlife. The Colima piece may have served as a burner lid, and its exact deposit is unknown. A similar shape can support different uses.
sections: The model is not the building
A possible vessel component

roman-world--palmyra.text: A Palmyrene funerary relief names kin. A Roman dynastic image presents a claim to legitimate rule. The earlier Egyptian portrait of Eutyches belongs to a different commemorative context and cannot stand for everyone living under Severan rule.
sections: A family claiming the right to rule
Names made a family memorable

palmyra--kushan-contexts.text: A tariff can identify recurring transactions at Palmyra, while a Kushan sanctuary inscription can identify responsibility for water and repairs. Network connections give them a wider setting, but neither record traces a particular family or coin between these places.
sections: The city regulated recurring transactions
A sanctuary had to be kept supplied

kushan-contexts--aksum.text: A Kushan coin’s imagery can reveal a ruler’s choices. Excavators at Beta Samati had five coins from different issues and checked their deposits against pottery and radiocarbon dates. A minting date alone cannot date the layer or tell how long a coin circulated.
sections: A small object carried a royal presentation
An old coin can occur in a later deposit

palmyra--aksum.text: Palmyra’s tariff documents local transactions. Aksum’s port, inland centre and excavated production sites show differing roles in an exchange system. Naming two trade centres supplies too little evidence to reconstruct an individual trader’s journey.
sections: The city regulated recurring transactions
Inland work sustained more than monuments

aksum--portuguese-voyage.text: Adulis linked the Aksumite highlands with Red Sea shipping. Many centuries later Portuguese ships sought access to existing commercial routes in the Indian Ocean. The two accounts support a comparison of port functions, while their dates rule out one continuous voyage.
sections: The inland city was not itself a harbor
A sea crossing depended on work near the shore

teotihuacan--moche.text: Blade-making debris in a Tlajinga compound and ceramic workshop evidence at Huacas de Moche put skilled production in specific places. Comparing these places does not identify the potter of a selected vessel or make the organization of the two cities identical.
sections: A household could also make tools
Making more than decorated bottles

dongson--shang-ritual.text: The miniature drum and Shang vessel demonstrate different ways of shaping and decorating bronze. A mould or a casting seam can answer a question about technique. Interpreting a frog or a vessel motif requires additional evidence specific to its setting.
sections: Making leaves evidence beyond the finished drum
Casting put several skills into one vessel

benin-ivory--ming-workshops.text: A Benin carver represented Portuguese figures on ivory tableware. The Ming jar can be placed in a reign-era ceramic tradition with court designs. The specific negotiations behind the ivory and the identity of the jar’s buyer require separate evidence.
sections: A customer’s request still needed a maker’s decisions
An official order needed more than a design

kongo-translation--mughal-books.text: The Kongo cross and bilingual catechism show how Christian imagery and words acquired local forms. A Mughal court project organized the translation and illustration of a sacred narrative. These records reveal different intermediaries and cannot establish every viewer’s belief.
sections: Translation required people who could question meanings
Language and patronage shaped an audience

manila-network--ming-workshops.text: Documented Pacific cargo and a later Mexican jar help explain how imported ceramics informed local work. The Ming jar shows a particular product. Its appearance gives no basis for putting that jar aboard the Manila wreck.
sections: Follow one interrupted voyage
Inspection and buying linked different organizations

banda-1621--haitian-revolution.text: The Banda letter casts violence through a colonial official reporting to superiors. In Haiti an abolition clause, labor rules and a declaration record different claims over freedom. Neither a colonial report nor a formal declaration supplies workers’ accounts of what followed.
sections: A monopoly claim became control over food and place
Ending slavery did not settle control of work

uruk-accounts--dholavira.text: At Uruk a tablet made selected goods or quantities available for accounting. At Dholavira waterworks and drains made stored water usable. Both imply organization, while the records cannot identify every worker’s status or measure each household’s access.
sections: A record separates a thing from its amount
A city needs water between rains

uruk-accounts--old-kingdom.text: A probable grain account from Uruk selects quantities and goods. An Old Kingdom chapel depicts offerings and activities for commemoration. An omission from a ledger or a scene gives little evidence about whether someone actually did that work.
sections: A record separates a thing from its amount
Providing for the dead

dholavira--liangzhu.text: Dholavira’s reservoirs and drains addressed water needs in an arid setting. Liangzhu’s channels and earthworks belonged to a rice-growing landscape. Engineering on either scale leaves open how labor was recruited or water allocated among households.
sections: A city needs water between rains
Engineering involved materials and repeated work

caral--skara-brae.text: At Caral construction fill and altered gathering spaces show repeated building work. At Skara Brae changes to entrances, passages and house interiors show maintenance where people lived. A preserved floor plan gives limited access to who planned or performed a renovation.
sections: Covering an old room made new construction possible
Rebuilding changed the available space

old-kingdom--caral.text: At Giza excavation, baking experiments and administrative records illuminate provisioning in different ways. At Caral successive fills show the work of renewing buildings. Bread production and building renewal both continued over time, but only particular tasks have documentary evidence.
sections: Grain was only a beginning
Covering an old room made new construction possible

old-kingdom--skara-brae.text: A funerary image in Egypt depicts activities chosen for remembrance. At Skara Brae rooms preserve evidence of occupation followed by rebuilding and modern conservation. The two records can be compared without treating either as a complete view of a working day.
sections: Providing for the dead
Rebuilding changed the available space

uluburun--shang-ritual.text: Uluburun preserved metal and finished goods in transit along with the ship that carried them. Shang moulds and vessels illuminate the work of casting. A stage of production seen in one case cannot supply the other object’s workshop, customer or travel history.
sections: One archaeological association, several kinds of work
Casting put several skills into one vessel

hattusha-change--uluburun.text: Store rooms and temples at Hattusha show institutions that needed supplies. Uluburun captures goods together in a single earlier shipment. Neither the cargo nor a later drought proxy can by itself explain the capital’s change in political fortunes.
sections: Food could be stored, but resilience had limits
One archaeological association, several kinds of work

kerma-potters--olmec.text: At Kerma, vessel surfaces and a recorded burial preserve particular evidence for ceramic skill and deposition. A small Olmec modeled body shows different decisions about form and finish. Style alone identifies neither its workshop nor an exchange link between these potters.
sections: Skilled hands controlled contrasting surfaces
A small body changes the question

lapita--polynesian-voyaging.text: Lapita pottery and settlement contexts trace movement and food procurement. Much later settlement dates and ancestral accounts in Aotearoa illuminate other voyages. Shared maritime skills cannot turn a decorative motif into one canoe’s route or a named ancestor’s itinerary.
sections: Settlement joined voyaging with provisioning
A small trace can test a large date claim

olmec--poverty-point.text: Olmec potters modeled a small figure. At Poverty Point people shaped local fine earth into objects that experiments show could be heated for cooking. Form records skilled choices, while a proposed use needs its own contextual or experimental test.
sections: A small body changes the question
Soil could help turn gathered food into meals

lapita--poverty-point.text: Lapita vessel decoration records one step in making a pot, while experiments with Poverty Point heating objects test a possible use. Moved materials within either region call for evidence of their own origin. These findings give no route between the Pacific and Louisiana.
sections: Potters also worked with local materials
Soil could help turn gathered food into meals

qin-administration--ashoka-messages.text: A Qin decree proclaimed a standard and excavated Liye records let readers inspect how officials handled documents. Ashoka’s edicts identify audiences and announced duties. Evidence for everyday implementation is much fuller in the selected Qin archive.
sections: A local office had to make records usable
Officials were told how to exercise power

ashoka-messages--athens-water.text: Ashoka’s edicts address officials and subjects, including work on practical provision. In Athens getting household water involved public places, while Assembly rights were restricted. A royal addressee and a person working in public had different kinds of access to power.
sections: The announced actions were practical
Water connected households with public space

nimrud-palace--ashoka-messages.text: Nimrud’s palace walls placed royal inscriptions and protective figures in particular rooms. Ashoka’s edicts varied by site, language and audience. Both rulers shaped a message in stone, while the voices of those moved or governed survive less directly in these sources.
sections: The king claims a city
A message needed a local audience

athens-water--qin-administration.text: Water carrying and commerce brought people excluded from the Athenian Assembly into public spaces. Qin documents preserve officials’ choices in applying rules. A painted scene cannot establish a woman’s legal position, just as a format variation cannot establish an official’s motive.
sections: Water connected households with public space
Uniformity had practical limits

taharqo--maya-vessel.text: A shabti names a Kushite king in a funerary setting. A Maya cup links an elite owner to imagery and drinking. What an object expresses about rank depends on its local use, and the selected examples give limited access to other households’ beliefs.
sections: Work imagined beyond life
Naming a relationship

chavin-textile--inca-weaving.text: The Chavín fragment combines a cotton weave with a painted design. The much later Inca tunic combines textile structures and camelid fibre. These technical differences are observable or catalogued. Neither garment’s maker or route is securely known.
sections: A surface was made before an image was painted
Start with the garment’s construction

byzantium--tang-city.text: Tang recruitment procedures document access for some educated men. A Byzantine devotional ivory offers a much narrower view of practice. Use dated evidence for a particular institution or object before asking how a capital changed over a long dynasty.
sections: Keeping the wider history in view
Walls and gates shaped an ordinary errand

abbasid-craft--song-art.text: Luster-painted Abbasid pottery and a Song glazed vessel show skilled work through their surfaces. Evidence for a painting commission or a court institution gives another view of patronage. The surviving objects alone do not identify who organized each workshop.
sections: The bowl’s surface required decisions and skill
A bowl begins with work, rather than a dynasty label

tang-city--abbasid-craft.text: Tang gates and recruitment rules shaped movement and access. Abbasid courts moved, while workshops and book copying depended on resources in particular cities. The better survival of Samarra compared with early Baghdad affects which activities can be documented.
sections: Walls and gates shaped an ordinary errand
Political authority changed before the final date

abbasid-craft--nalanda.text: Copying books and making pottery in Abbasid settings required skilled people and supplies. At Nalanda endowed land, residence and teaching supported monastic learning. An excavation and a visitor’s account preserve different parts of those arrangements.
sections: Books also depended on skilled production
Learning required support beyond a teaching hall

borobudur--nalanda.text: Borobudur’s terraces and carved reliefs organized movement among religious images. At Nalanda rooms and buildings supported a residential learning community. Rebuilding and modern conservation make an exact reconstruction of either place at one date difficult.
sections: Moving water required continued work
Learning required support beyond a teaching hall

mali-networks--middle-niger.text: Accounts of Mali describe rulers and communities with varying autonomy. Archaeologists have interpreted Middle Niger settlement networks without presuming one centralized hierarchy. A dated terracotta figure cannot identify a ruler or define how that region was governed.
sections: Cities had histories before this empire
Organization is a question to investigate

song-art--inca-weaving.text: The Song fiscal proposal described the hoped-for benefit of borrowing and tax arrangements. Inca rotating service and provisioning raise questions about actual returns to workers. Neither a proposal nor a finished tunic measures how a household experienced an obligation.
sections: A proposal tried to alter the timing of debt
Work could be demanded in different ways

portuguese-voyage--benin-ivory.text: A voyage narrative names pilots, envoys and interpreters and records detention. The later Benin ivory preserves an Edo carver’s choices for a distant client. A captain’s itinerary cannot reconstruct that commission, its payment or the maker’s instructions.
sections: Help and coercion appear in the same account
A customer’s request still needed a maker’s decisions

portuguese-voyage--kongo-translation.text: Interpreters and pilots enabled the Portuguese voyage, sometimes under constraint. Kongo students, clergy and artists reshaped Christian communication, while royal letters sought action on trafficking. Translation and a request for protection give different evidence of choice and enforcement.
sections: Calicut required several kinds of interpretation
Afonso’s letters sought a response to kidnapping

mali-networks--inca-weaving.text: A foreign image of a wealthy ruler makes the labor supporting Mali’s exchanges difficult to see. An Inca tunic preserves textile skill, while other sources describe service and provisioning. Neither object specifies what its workers owed or received.
sections: A pilgrimage and a later map have separate dates
Work could be demanded in different ways

angkor--dholavira.text: At Dholavira reservoirs and drains show how people captured seasonal water. At Angkor successive waterways linked settlements and fields, and researchers model how failures could spread. Neither a reservoir nor a network model identifies every household’s access or a single cause of urban change.
sections: How a water network works
Read components before drawing a complete system

factory-reform--hine-labor.text: A British inspection report records how one complaint was handled. Hine’s American mill photograph and caption document a reform investigation. Establishing workers’ hours, ages or improved protection requires employment and enforcement records beyond either account.
sections: An inspector had to investigate what happened
A rule needed records and inspectors

tomioka--hine-labor.text: Tomioka’s reeling machines depended on trained workers and a silk supply. Hine’s cotton-mill image captures a workplace selected for a reform investigation. A reconstructed training history and a photograph give unequal access to the workers’ experiences.
sections: A machine still needs practiced hands
A caption records a contested explanation

tiriti--partition-1947.text: Te Tiriti’s different texts and the history of signings and refusals complicate claims about consent. At partition political decisions and border timetables affected people with little control over them. A signatory list or a military letter can represent only particular voices.
sections: Sheets record different decisions
Why Punjab and Bengal need separate attention

partition-1947--south-africa-rights.text: The partition timetable and correspondence can be compared with accounts of displacement. South Africa’s constitution and election materials record different commitments and procedures. Each political transition needs separate evidence before its effects on daily life can be measured.
sections: What an official report can reveal
A majority needed constitutional limits

world-war-one--world-war-two.text: First World War recruiting material shows how governments sought people for imperial war. Orders, occupation records and testimony illuminate the distinct machinery of Nazi persecution and genocide. A recruiting appeal cannot explain why an individual enlisted or substitute for evidence of targeted killing.
sections: A public appeal does not measure its own success
Name the crime accurately

sputnik--tomioka.text: Tomioka’s mill relied on silk growers, trained reelers and machinery. Sputnik’s launch required transmitters, power, orbit calculations and observers. Both cases identify work behind a technical achievement, while the evidence for a mill worker and a launch planner differs sharply.
sections: A signal depended on work on Earth
A machine still needs practiced hands

poverty-point--hopewell-earthworks.text: Poverty Point builders moved earth and maintained a shared plaza. In the Ohio Hopewell networks, households could gather at ceremonial enclosures. The scale of construction supplies evidence for cooperation but cannot distinguish permanent residence or form of government by itself.
sections: Moving earth required a sequence of tasks
Shared places and everyday provision

chaco-communities--cahokia-city.text: Chaco masonry and food evidence address how people provisioned gatherings. At Cahokia homes, public buildings and local soil records trace changing neighborhoods. A later photograph or contemporary community statement needs its own date when interpreting ancient patterns.
sections: Food connected fields, storage and gathering
Homes within an urban landscape

ottoman-workshops--isfahan-silk.text: Ottoman court specialists and ceramic makers worked for multiple patrons and markets. Isfahan’s silk economy also included rural producers and merchants affected by coerced Armenian relocation. A surviving dish or carpet cannot measure the benefits to those workers.
sections: Work for patrons and buyers
A prosperous quarter followed forced movement

bukhara-books--zand-iran.text: An illustrated book from Bukhara preserves a patronage context and separates copying from painting. A Zand lacquer case has an attributed maker, but its purchaser is unknown. Differences between those records limit what can be inferred about changes in buyers’ tastes.
sections: A book made through several acts
One object, several kinds of evidence

bering-sea-carvers--inuinnait-sewing.text: A carved Bering Sea ivory component shows fitting and engraving but cannot recover a whole hunt. For Inuinnait sewing, a historical photograph and a later community-led reconstruction illuminate different stages of inquiry. The two cases are separated by many centuries.
sections: A component, not the whole hunting system
Makers research and teach

ozette-makah--kwakwakawakw-potlatch.text: Makah oral history and excavation give the recovered Ozette household materials a community setting. Kwakwaka’wakw histories of confiscation and return explain separate responsibilities surrounding potlatch belongings. Evidence that an object survived cannot establish who had authority over its use.
sections: Belongings stayed in the community
Return required organization and family decisions

blackfoot-bison--hidatsa-villages.text: Blackfoot accounts connect coordinated bison hunting with obligations extending beyond the kill. Hidatsa gardens, storage and women’s roles in earthlodge construction show work over a village year. Each account places hunting and seasonal knowledge within a particular community.
sections: Seasonal work and respectful relations connected households
An earthlodge joined construction with household authority

ocmulgee-council--wendat-laine.text: Ocmulgee’s clay remains and revised construction dates concern a particular earthlodge. At the Wendat site of Laine, a modeled date range estimates village occupation. Neither a revised sample nor a probability plot supplies a precise founding date for a people.
sections: Retained material makes new questions possible
Two date clusters do not make a century-long village

haudenosaunee-canandaigua--cherokee-prin.text: Canandaigua treaty clauses document commitments whose fulfillment must be investigated. Cherokee-language print enabled national debate during the approach to removal. A treaty image and a newspaper each preserve political words without recording universal agreement or implementation.
sections: A continuing relationship requires particular evidence
Political defense coexisted with enslavement and exclusion

ojibwe-manoomin--inuinnait-sewing.text: Ojibwe accounts place ricing and the finishing of manoomin within relationships of responsibility. Inuinnait sewing combines learned techniques with changing materials. Photographs and later reconstructions have separate dates and can reveal different parts of that knowledge.
sections: Harvested grain still needed several kinds of work
Makers research and teach

nimrud-palace--taharqo.text: The Nimrud palace required quarrying, carving and continuing service. Taharqo’s Kawa texts claim royal organization, while workshop debris at Sanam records faience making. Royal language and the excavation of a workshop give different access to workers’ status and choices.
sections: Making a royal centre
A workshop makes the connection tangible

kerma-potters--taharqo.text: Kerma’s pottery and excavated craft areas relate differently to production than a royal shabti does. A faience fragment matches the Sanam mould, while the selected granite figure is only probably associated with Nuri. Geographic proximity cannot supply its workshop or a continuous labor system.
sections: An Egyptian findspot opens a further question
A workshop makes the connection tangible
